title: Project: a Caesar cipher
summary: Build a small encryption program from functions you can test, then break it by brute force.

sources.section: The join() and split() String Methods

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner

steps.title: From features to a whole program
steps.body:
So far each lesson taught one feature. Real programs combine them. In this project you build a
tiny encryption tool, the **Caesar cipher**, which hides a message by moving every letter a fixed
number of places along the alphabet. It needs strings, loops, conditions and functions working
together, and it is small enough to finish, test and then break.

steps.title: Letters on a wheel
steps.body:
Picture the 26 letters written around a wheel. The **key** says how many places to turn it: with key
3, A becomes D and B becomes E. At the end the wheel wraps round, so X, Y and Z become A, B and C.
In code the wheel is a position number from 0 to 25, and "wrap round" is the remainder after
dividing by 26: `(position + key) % 26`. Turning the wheel back the other way undoes it.

questions: If the key is 26, what does the message look like after encryption?
How many different keys are really possible? What does that mean for someone trying to read your secret?

steps.title: Watch one letter wrap round
steps.body: Y is near the end of the alphabet, so shifting it by 3 has to wrap.

visual.code:
ALPHABET = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def shift_letter(ch, key):
    pos = ALPHABET.index(ch)
    return ALPHABET[(pos + key) % 26]

print(shift_letter("Y", 3))

frames.note: `index` finds where Y sits: position 24 (A is 0).
24 + 3 = 27 is past the end; 27 % 26 = 1 wraps to the start.

steps.title: The pieces you need
steps.body:
**Remainder:** `a % n` is what is left after dividing `a` by `n`. For a positive `n` the answer is
always between `0` and `n - 1`, even when `a` is negative: `-3 % 26` is `23`. That is why shifting by
`-key` correctly turns the wheel back.

**Finding a position:** `text.index(ch)` gives the position of the first `ch` in `text`, and raises
`ValueError` if it is missing, so check `ch in text` first. `message.upper()` gives an upper-case copy.

**Building the result:** collect the pieces in a list and finish with `"".join(pieces)`, which glues
a list of strings into one string.

**Program design:** give each job its own small function (`encrypt`, `decrypt`, `crack`). Each one
can then be tested on its own, and later functions reuse earlier ones.

steps.title: Run it: encrypt and back
steps.body: Characters that are not letters pass through unchanged. Predict the last line before you run it.
steps.expected_output:
PHHW DW QRRQ!
MEET AT NOON!
23

steps.title: Your turn: decrypt
steps.body:
`encrypt` is done. Complete `decrypt(message, key)` so it undoes `encrypt` with the same key. Reuse
`encrypt` rather than writing the loop again.
hints: Decrypting with key 3 means turning the wheel 3 places the other way.
`encrypt(message, -key)` turns it backwards; `%` handles the negative number for you.

tests.name: round trip for every key
tests.code:
for k in range(0, 60):
    assert decrypt(encrypt('HELLO, WORLD', k), k) == 'HELLO, WORLD', f'key {k} does not round-trip'

tests.name: reuses encrypt

steps.title: Challenge: break the cipher
steps.body:
With only 26 possible keys, an attacker can simply try them all. Write `crack(ciphertext, words)`:
try every key from 0 to 25, score each decryption by how many of its space-separated words are in
the set `words`, and return `(key, plaintext)` for the best score. If keys tie, keep the smallest.
hints: Loop `for key in range(26):` and call `decrypt(ciphertext, key)`.
Score with `sum(1 for w in plain.split() if w in words)`; remember the best key so far, replacing it only on a strictly higher score.

tests.name: finds key 3
tests.code: assert crack('PHHW DW QRRQ', {'MEET', 'AT', 'NOON'}) == (3, 'MEET AT NOON'), f"got {crack('PHHW DW QRRQ', {'MEET', 'AT', 'NOON'})!r}"

tests.name: key 0 is a candidate
tests.code: assert crack('HELLO THERE', {'HELLO', 'THERE'}) == (0, 'HELLO THERE'), 'try key 0 as well'

tests.name: best score wins, not the first match
tests.code:
c = encrypt('THE CAT SAT', 13)
assert crack(c, {'THE', 'CAT', 'SAT', 'GUR'}) == (13, 'THE CAT SAT'), 'key 0 matches one word, key 13 matches three'

tests.name: ties keep the smallest key
tests.code: assert crack('XYZ', set()) == (0, 'XYZ'), 'with no matches at all, every key ties: return key 0'

questions.explanation: With a positive divisor, Python's `%` gives an answer from 0 to 25, so one step back from A lands on Z (25).

questions.prompt: Why does trying every key break a Caesar cipher so easily?
choices: There are only 26 keys to try
The key is stored inside the message
questions.explanation: A search over 26 candidates finishes instantly; real ciphers have far too many keys for this.
A moves to B, the dash is kept, and Z wraps round to A.

steps.title: What you built
steps.body:
- A cipher made of small functions that each do one job and can be tested alone.
- `%` to wrap positions round, including negative shifts for decryption.
- `index`, `in` and `"".join(...)` to move between letters, positions and strings.
- A brute-force search that scores every candidate and keeps the best.

Try next: the ROT13 cipher uses key 13, so encrypting twice gets the message back. Can you see why?
